meta.description: Rules for correcting the neutral sentiment bias and flat emotional expression characteristic of AI text. Human writing embeds emotional layers that evolve organically; AI sentiment is based on statistical patterns rather than experiential grounding.
meta.usage: Third pass, after lexical and structural. Call humanizer_get_sentiment_tone. Context-dependent: tone changes risk altering meaning more than lexical or structural changes do, so apply only when the rewrite scope explicitly permits tone shifts (e.g., not for objective reporting). Respect absolute_rules AR-001 (preserve original meaning, intent, claims, stance) when softening or sharpening tone.
meta.research_basis: Muñoz-Ortiz et al. (2024) emotion analysis across six LLMs showed AI skews toward neutral/positive sentiment while humans express more anger, disgust, and fear. Gillham (2024) confirmed LLM-generated articles cluster near neutral on the sentiment scale. Opara (2025) demonstrated that human emotional expression is layered and progressive while AI emotion is flat and stereotyped.

neutral_bias.ai_pattern: LLM-generated text is closer to the neutral part of the sentiment scale. It demonstrates a slightly higher inclination toward neutrality compared to human text, with less expression of aggressive negative emotions like anger, disgust, and fear. AI tends to generate more texts imbued with positive emotions such as surprise and joy.
neutral_bias.human_pattern: Human text demonstrates a greater inclination toward negative and aggressive emotions like disgust and fear. Humans express a wider range of sentiment with more dynamic variation across paragraphs.

rules.rule: Do not sand down strong opinions into balanced summaries.
rules.guidance: If the content expresses a position, let it express that position with conviction. AI defaults to 'on the other hand' balance even when the text doesn't call for it.

Frustration, skepticism, disappointment, and concern are all human emotions that AI tends to soften. 'This approach has serious problems' is more human than 'This approach presents certain challenges that merit consideration.'

rules.rule: Keep the sentiment shifts the source has.
rules.guidance: Where the source shifts register from one paragraph to the next (enthusiastic, then cautious, then blunt), keep each shift and do not flatten them into one steady tone. Add no shift the source does not make (absolute_rules AR-001).

emotional_layering.ai_pattern: AI-generated sentiment expressions often appear flat, stereotyped, or overly uniform. When AI attempts to convey emotion, it does so through predictable linguistic choices without dynamic progression. The emotion arrives all at once rather than building.
emotional_layering.human_pattern: Human authors naturally embed emotional layers in their writing, drawing from lived experience, empathy, and reflective processes. Emotional expression evolves organically within the text, showing contextual variation and dynamic sentiment progression.

rules.rule: Build emotional intensity gradually rather than stating it.
rules.guidance: Instead of 'This was a deeply frustrating experience,' show the frustration building through increasingly specific detail and shorter, sharper sentences.

rules.rule: Mix emotional registers within a passage.
rules.guidance: Human writers combine humor with seriousness, enthusiasm with caution, confidence with vulnerability, often within the same paragraph. AI keeps these registers separate.

rules.rule: Use emotion words sparingly but precisely.
rules.guidance: Human text has high emotion word count but embeds it in layers. Rather than labeling an emotion ('I felt angry'), human writers describe the experience that produces the emotion and let the reader feel it.
Human writing reflects the author's position. AI defaults to objective reporting. Where the content type allows it (opinion, analysis, marketing), let the writer's stance come through.

rules.rule: Use an exclamation mark only where the content carries surprise or excitement.
rules.guidance: Model prose rarely uses exclamation marks. In informal, marketing or conversational content, one placed where the source's feeling calls for it reads as human. 'The fix worked!' reads as more human than 'The fix was successful.' Keep them out of formal and academic prose. A string of them is its own tell.

subjectivity.ai_pattern: AI text tends toward objective, impersonal language. It minimizes first-person perspective, avoids direct opinions, and presents information from a neutral, omniscient standpoint.
subjectivity.human_pattern: Human text varies between subjective and objective registers depending on context. Even in formal writing, human authors insert personal evaluation, qualification based on experience, and markers of individual judgment.

rules.rule: Use the first person only where the user or the source supplies the position or experience.
rules.guidance: A phrase like 'In my experience' or 'I'd argue' belongs in the draft only when the user or the source supplies the experience or the position behind it. Never invent one to make the text sound human (see absolute_rules AR-001).

rules.rule: State the evaluation the source or the user holds.
rules.guidance: 'Interesting,' 'surprising,' 'disappointing,' 'overdue': words like these carry the writer's assessment. Where the source or the user makes a judgment, keep it in an evaluative word; AI drafts tend to flatten it into a neutral description. Do not add a judgment the source does not make (see absolute_rules AR-001).

rules.rule: Base each hedge on a limit the writer knows.
rules.guidance: Human hedging says 'I'm not sure this holds for every case'; it's specific and based on knowledge limits. AI hedging says 'Generally speaking'; it's formulaic and universal. Where the source states the limit behind a formulaic hedge, use it; otherwise swap the formula for a plain word that marks the same limit (absolute_rules AR-001).

sensing_and_experience_language.description: Human text uses more sensing verbs and experience-based language that AI tends to avoid.
rewriting_guidance: Reintroduce sensory and experiential language where the content allows it.

Where the source gives the concrete observation behind an abstract description, use it. If the notes say the buttons are tiny and the labels overlap, 'The interface has usability issues' → 'The buttons are tiny and the labels overlap.' Do not invent the observation (absolute_rules AR-001).
Use verbs of perception: 'It looks like,' 'This reads as.' These signal embodied experience.

readability.description: AI text often reads harder than its audience needs. Human writers adjust complexity to their reader; AI writes at a uniformly elevated register.
readability.ai_pattern: AI defaults to longer words, complex sentence structures, and formal vocabulary regardless of the target audience. A blog post reads at the same grade level as an academic paper.
readability.human_pattern: Human writers calibrate. A newsletter aimed at general audiences uses shorter sentences and simpler words than a research paper. Even within a single document, humans simplify when explaining and complexify when analyzing.

rules.rule: Match readability to the content type and audience.
rules.guidance: Write for the reader the piece is for. A blog post or a marketing page should read more easily than a professional report, and a report more easily than a research paper. If the text reads harder than its audience expects, simplify.

rules.rule: Let the difficulty of a passage follow its job.
rules.guidance: Human writers simplify where they explain and let analysis run denser. An introduction often reads more easily than the technical core because its reader needs the way in.

rules.rule: Prefer short, common words when meaning is clear from context.
rules.guidance: If the surrounding sentences have already established the topic, shorter words carry no ambiguity. 'Use' instead of 'utilize'. 'Show' instead of 'demonstrate'. 'Help' instead of 'facilitate'. The context does the heavy lifting; the word just needs to point.

readability.research_basis: Markowitz et al. (2023) find AI produces lower readability scores than human text. Opara (2025) identifies FleschReadingEase and GunningFog as discriminating features in the StyloAI framework.
